q2-153.n: Allah made patience and prayer two aids to be relied on in every hardship, and promised the patient His special companionship: the companionship of help, support and steadfastness.

q2-155.n: Trial is an established law in fear, provision and life; the way out is not denying the pain but relating it back to Allah: “Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return” — and its reward is blessings from Allah, mercy and guidance.

q2-286.n: What Allah has charged you with is within your capacity, and what is beyond your capacity is not asked of you — a principle that eases self-blame and anxiety about falling short.

q2-216.n: A person's knowledge of outcomes is limited, so do not judge a painful event to be pure evil; the verse opens the door to contentment without cancelling effort.

q94-5.n: The commentators said: “hardship” comes with the definite article and “ease” without it, so the hardship is one and the ease is many — one hardship will not overcome two eases. And ease comes “with” hardship, not only after it.

q65-2.n: Piety is the key to ways out and to provision, and trust in Allah is sufficiency. The verse ends “Allah has already set for everything a decreed extent,” teaching that relief has an appointed time, so do not be impatient.

q65-7.n: A clear promise that hardship is not the end of the road, revealed in the context of spending and financial difficulty.

q39-10.n: Every deed has a measured reward except patience, whose reward is without account — and this gives long suffering meaning and value.

q29-2.n: Trial is neither a sign of anger nor a proof of abandonment; it is a law for sifting out the truthful. Those before you went through the same.

q57-22.n: Believing in the decree protects from two extremes: the crippling grief over what has been lost, and the arrogant joy over what has been gained.

q64-11.n: ‘Alqamah said: It is the man struck by a calamity who knows it is from Allah, so he is content and submits. The reward mentioned is guidance of the heart: calm and understanding.

q12-18.n: Beautiful patience is patience without complaining to people, while seeking Allah's help; Ya'qub said it when his sons lied to him.

q12-86.n: Complaining to Allah does not contradict patience, and weeping does not contradict contentment; Ya'qub's eyes turned white from grief while his hope stayed alive.

q12-87.n: Ya'qub combined the command to strive — “go and find out” — with the prohibition of despair; true hope pushes towards action, not passive waiting.

q12-90.n: The essence of Yusuf's story as he himself summed it up: piety and patience, and the good outcome belongs to those who do good, however long the road.

q12-92.n: Yusuf forgave his brothers at the moment of complete power, without taunting them or reminding them of the past; and the Prophet ﷺ quoted it on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

q12-100.n: From Yusuf's refinement: he mentioned the prison and not the well so as not to embarrass his brothers, and attributed the rift to Satan's interference rather than to any malice in them.

q21-83.n: Ayyub's supplication is a model of how to complain: describing his state — “adversity has touched me” — and mentioning Allah's mercy, without objecting or dictating.

q21-87.n: Three layers of darkness — the night, the sea and the belly of the whale — yet he was saved through declaring Allah's oneness and admitting his fault. “And thus do We save the believers” extends the promise to everyone in distress.

q38-44.n: Allah praised Ayyub for patience and for turning back to Him, even though he complained to Allah; complaining to the Creator does not break patience.

q19-23.n: A sincere moment of human weakness from a truthful woman, which Allah met with reassurance, then with a command to take a simple means — “shake the trunk” — and then with care for her body — “eat and drink”.

q9-40.n: Tranquillity descends with certainty that Allah is with you, and true companionship is part of steadfastness.

q3-139.n: Revealed after the defeat at Uhud: do not let a temporary loss break your spirit and your dignity.

q3-173.n: “Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs” — Ibrahim said it when he was thrown into the fire, and the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions said it when they were threatened; and the outcome was blessing and favour.

q13-28.n: Tranquillity is not the absence of problems but the heart resting in Allah in the midst of them, and remembrance is its direct path.

q20-25.n: Musa's supplication before the hardest mission of his life: he asked for an open heart before asking for the matter to be made easy, and for help in expressing himself.

q20-46.n: Allah's answer to Musa and Harun when they said “we are afraid that he will hasten punishment against us or transgress”: natural fear is not blamed, and its cure is remembering that Allah is with you.

q26-61.n: The sea in front and the enemy behind, and every calculation said “we are sure to be overtaken” — but certainty said “No!” Then relief came from where no one expected.

q28-7.n: The mother takes the means and then entrusts her child to Allah; He forbade her both fear (of the future) and grief (over the separation).

q27-62.n: Desperation brings the answer nearer; times of severe distress are times of the most sincere supplication.

q2-186.n: Allah did not say “then say: I am near” but answered directly “indeed I am near,” a sign that there is no intermediary between the servant and his Lord in supplication.

q40-60.n: Supplication is an act of worship that is commanded, with a promise of response — and the response may be by giving, by averting harm, or by storing reward.

q93-3.n: Revealed when revelation paused and the idolaters said “his Lord has forsaken him”; it is a cure for the feeling of being abandoned: Allah has not left you.

q15-97.n: Allah knows how your chest tightens at what people say, and the remedy offered is glorification, prostration and continuing in worship, not getting caught up in replying.

q16-127.n: Patience itself is a gift from Allah to be asked of Him, along with a warning against being overly preoccupied with people's schemes.

q10-62.n: Being close to Allah is not a supernatural rank but faith and piety, and its fruit is safety from fear and grief.

q11-115.n: When people do not see your effort, Allah does not let it go to waste.

q2-214.n: Even the Messenger and the believers with him were so distressed that they said “When is the help of Allah?” — the question is not weak faith, and the answer is: it is near.

q9-51.n: Certainty that what is written for you will not miss you frees the heart from chronic anxiety about the future.

q3-200.n: Three levels: patience with oneself, persevering patience over a long road and in facing the opponent, and remaining stationed — standing firm in one's position.

q39-53.n: The most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah according to many of the early scholars: He addressed the transgressors as “O My servants”, never removing their belonging to Him.

q3-135.n: Among the qualities of the pious is that they may fall into sin, but the difference is that they return quickly and do not persist.

q25-70.n: Sincere repentance does not only erase the past; it turns it into good deeds, so the past no longer remains a chain.

q11-114.n: Revealed about a man who kissed a woman and came full of regret (al-Bukhari 526): good deeds erase bad deeds, and the cure is positive action, not regret alone.

q4-110.n: The door of forgiveness is open for every sin, with sincere seeking of forgiveness.

q66-8.n: Sincere repentance: regret for what has passed, stopping now, resolving not to return, and returning people's rights if they are involved.

q20-82.n: The intensive form “Ghaffar” means abundant and repeated forgiveness, for the one whose repentance is repeated.

q7-23.n: The first repentance in human history: admission without justification — unlike Iblis, who justified his disobedience.

q71-10.n: The Quran links seeking forgiveness with abundant provision and offspring; al-Hasan al-Basri used to advise those who complained of drought, poverty or having few children to seek forgiveness.

q15-49.n: Balance between hope and fear: forgiveness and mercy come first, then the reminder of punishment, so that hope does not turn into carelessness.

q7-156.n: Allah's mercy is vaster than any sin and any circumstance.

q6-54.n: Whoever disobeys Allah does so in ignorance (of the consequences), as the early scholars said, and setting things right after repentance is a condition of completing it.

q42-40.n: Three levels: justice (the equivalent), virtue (forgiveness with reconciliation), and injustice (going beyond), which Allah does not love. Praiseworthy forgiveness is that which is accompanied by setting things right.

q42-43.n: Patience in the face of harm and forgiving are among “the matters requiring determination”: they need strength of will, not weakness.

q42-37.n: He did not praise them for never getting angry, but for forgiving when they are angry; anger is nature, forgiveness is a choice.

q41-34.n: A Quranic strategy for turning an enemy into a friend: responding with what is better, not with the same — while admitting it is hard and only the patient can do it.

q24-22.n: Revealed about Abu Bakr when he swore not to spend on his relative Mistah after he joined in the slander; he said: “Yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me,” and resumed his spending.

q7-199.n: A comprehensive rule for dealing with people: accept from them what comes easily of their character, enjoin what is good, turn away from the ignorant, and seek refuge with Allah when anger stirs.

q25-63.n: “Peace” means words by which they remain free of sin; they do not match the foolish in their foolishness.

q16-126.n: The Quran permits retaliation with the equivalent as justice, then encourages patience because it is better; you are free to choose between your right and what is better.

q64-14.n: Even within the family harm may come, and what is asked is caution together with pardon, overlooking and forgiveness — not cutting ties.

q15-85.n: Gracious forgiveness: forgiveness without reproach, harm or reminding of favours.

q59-10.n: A supplication to purify the heart of rancour and resentment; a sound heart is not achieved by willpower alone, but by supplication too.

q5-8.n: Your dislike of a person or a people does not permit you to wrong them; justice with an opponent is the true test of piety.

q16-90.n: Ibn Mas‘ud said: It is the most comprehensive verse in the Quran for good and evil. Justice is the foundation, and excellence rises above it.

q14-42.n: Delaying punishment is neither heedlessness nor neglect; it is consolation for the wronged and a warning to the wrongdoer.

q42-41.n: Claiming your right after being wronged is legitimate and blameless; forgiveness is a virtue, not an obligation.

q4-148.n: The wronged person may complain of the injustice and mention the wrongdoer's deed to someone who can give justice, and this is not forbidden backbiting.

q6-164.n: No one bears another's sin: do not punish a son for his father's sin, or a family for one member's mistake.

q6-152.n: Justice in speech and testimony, even towards relatives.

q4-58.n: Every responsibility is a trust: money, position, secrets and words.

q17-34.n: Promises and contracts are a responsibility a person will be asked about before Allah.

q28-26.n: A Quranic criterion for hiring and choosing: competence (“the strong”) and trustworthiness together.

q66-11.n: Pharaoh's wife lived in the house of a tyrant, so she asked for the Neighbour before the house — “near You” — and asked to be saved; praying to escape an environment of oppression is legitimate.

q28-21.n: Leaving a dangerous environment is taking the means and does not contradict trust in Allah; Musa left afraid, and he prayed.

q49-6.n: The method of verifying before judging: no decision should be built on an unreliable report, or regret will follow.

q49-10.n: Reconciling people in dispute is one of the greatest acts of devotion, and mercy is the fruit of fearing Allah in disputes.

q49-11.n: Ridicule, defamation and hurtful nicknames are forbidden, and “do not defame yourselves” means your brother is like yourself: whoever insults him insults himself.

q49-12.n: Three links in a chain: suspicion leads to spying, spying exposes faults, and then comes backbiting; the Quran cuts the chain at its start.

q49-13.n: The measure of honour before Allah is piety, not lineage, colour or wealth — the basis for rejecting racism and boasting.

q17-53.n: He did not say “what is good” but “that which is best”: choose the best possible words, because Satan exploits harsh words to sow enmity.

q2-83.n: The command to speak well is general to all people, believers and others.

q24-15.n: “You received it with your tongues” — not your ears: a picture of how fast a rumour spreads before it passes through the mind.

q24-12.n: The first duty on hearing an accusation: think well of the accused as you would of yourself, and do not pass the talk on.

q24-11.n: Even a false accusation carries good for the wronged: reward, the separating of the truthful from the hypocrite, and a greater vindication.

q50-18.n: Every word is recorded; remembering this before speaking is a cure for backbiting and slips of the tongue.

q4-114.n: Private conversations hold no good except what concerns charity, kindness or reconciliation — so make your private talk about setting things right.

q16-125.n: Dialogue with those who differ is by wisdom, good counsel and arguing in the best way — not by harshness and wounding words.

q20-44.n: If Musa was commanded to be gentle with the tyrant Pharaoh, then gentleness with a parent, spouse or friend is even more fitting.

q31-18.n: Luqman's guidance to his son on humility and lowering the voice; raising your voice in an argument does not make your case any stronger.

q33-70.n: Right speech: truthful, upright and on target; its fruit is that one's deeds are set right.

q61-2.n: A contradiction between words and actions robs words of their effect, especially for a parent, teacher or leader.

q4-86.n: A principle of conduct: answer a greeting or a kind gesture with something better.

q2-263.n: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by reminders or hurt.

q17-23.n: Kindness to parents is joined to the worship of Allah alone, and old age is singled out because it is a time of weakness and short patience; even saying “uff” is forbidden.

q31-14.n: Even parents who pressure their child about the gravest matter (associating partners with Allah) are to be accompanied with kindness; obedience is in what is right, and honouring them never falls away.

q46-15.n: The supplication of one who reaches forty: gratitude for the blessings on him and his parents, asking for righteous offspring, and renewing repentance.

q19-43.n: Ibrahim kept saying “O my father” gently, and when his father threatened to stone him he replied “Peace be upon you”; disagreeing on the greatest issues does not cancel good manners.

q30-21.n: The aims of marriage: tranquillity, affection and mercy. Some commentators said: affection is in youth and mercy in old age; when affection weakens, mercy remains.

q4-19.n: Living together in kindness is required even when there is dislike, and passing dislike is no justification for tearing a marriage down.

q4-35.n: A Quranic mechanism for resolving marital conflict: wise mediation from both sides, and a sincere intention to reconcile is the condition for success.

q4-128.n: “And reconciliation is best” is a general rule: settlement and mutual concession are better than a rift.

q2-237.n: Revealed in the context of divorce: even at separation, do not forget the goodness and kindness that were between you.

q2-187.n: Spouses are a covering, a refuge and closeness for each other; each conceals the other's faults and protects them.

q2-229.n: If the marriage continues, it is with kindness; if it ends, it is with good treatment — there is no place for causing harm in either case.

q25-74.n: The supplication of the servants of the Most Merciful for their family: that it be a comfort to the eyes — a source of peace and joy.

q66-6.n: The responsibility of upbringing begins with oneself — “yourselves” — before the family: example before instruction.

q31-13.n: A Quranic model for advising children: calling them affectionately “O my son”, starting with the foundations, giving reasons for commands, and linking it all to patience.

q20-132.n: “And be steadfast” in the intensive form: upbringing needs long, repeated patience, not a single command.

q18-46.n: Wealth and children are adornment, not the goal; what lasts is righteous deeds.

q4-1.n: Ties of kinship are mentioned alongside Allah's name in the command to be conscious of Him, showing how great their bond is.

q47-22.n: Cutting ties of kinship is paired with spreading corruption on earth.

q13-21.n: Among the qualities of people of understanding is joining what Allah has commanded to be joined, foremost the ties of kinship.

q4-36.n: The ten circles of kindness: from parents to the distant neighbour and the companion in travel and work.

q28-56.n: Revealed about Abu Talib: the Prophet ﷺ himself could not guide the person he loved most. Your part is to convey and to be kind; guidance belongs to Allah.

q88-21.n: Your role is to remind, not to control other people's hearts.

q18-6.n: A merciful reproach to the Prophet ﷺ for grieving so deeply over those who did not respond; do not destroy yourself with sorrow over other people's choices.

q2-256.n: Faith cannot be imposed by compulsion; clarity is the way.

q60-8.n: Kindness and justice towards non-Muslims who live in peace is legitimate and loved by Allah.

q11-6.n: Provision for every living creature is guaranteed by Allah; this does not cancel effort but lifts the anxiety from it.

q51-22.n: Allah swore by provision as surely as you are certain of your own speech — an assurance that cuts off the whispering fear of poverty.

q2-280.n: The right of a debtor in hardship to be given time is obligatory, and remitting the debt is a better charity.

q2-268.n: Excessive fear of poverty is a satanic whisper that pushes towards stinginess or the unlawful, while Allah promises forgiveness and bounty.

q34-39.n: Spending in good does not decrease wealth; it is replaced.

q14-7.n: Gratitude brings increase, and it begins with noticing the blessing you have before asking for what you lack.

q67-15.n: The command to walk the earth in search of provision: effort is worship, and trust in Allah does not mean sitting idle.

q62-10.n: Balance between worship and work: prayer, then dispersing to seek provision while remembering Allah.

q4-32.n: The cure for envy: instead of wishing for what others have, work for your own share and ask Allah of His vast bounty.

q20-131.n: Constantly looking at what others have spoils contentment; what they have is a “flower”, beautiful but quick to wither.

q113-5.n: A surah for seeking refuge from external evils, including envy; the Prophet ﷺ used to recite the last two surahs and seek protection by them.

q17-29.n: Financial moderation: neither stinginess nor extravagance that leads to regret and debt.

q25-67.n: Among the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful is balance in spending.

q28-24.n: Musa was a hungry stranger without work, yet he helped others first and then prayed; work, marriage and safety came to him after that.

q59-9.n: Preferring others at a time of need is the height of generosity, and success lies in being protected from the stinginess of the soul.

q76-8.n: Whoever works for Allah's sake is not crushed when he is not thanked, for he never expected thanks from the start.

q93-9.n: Whoever has tasted being orphaned and in need (as the Prophet ﷺ did) is most fitting to be gentle with orphans and the needy.

q5-2.n: The measure for cooperation at work and in friendship: cooperate in what is righteous, and not in what is sinful.

q83-1.n: Giving short measure includes anyone who demands his full right while shortchanging others' rights — in trade, work and evaluation.

q53-39.n: Results are tied to effort, and effort itself is preserved and seen by Allah even if the result is not complete.

q9-105.n: Your work is seen by Allah even if your manager or people do not see it.

q13-11.n: Change begins from within: convictions, habits and intention.

q29-69.n: Striving is the condition for being guided to the ways; every sincere step is met with a path opening.

q3-159.n: A complete method of leadership: gentleness, then forgiveness, then seeking forgiveness for others, then consultation, then resolve, then trust in Allah.

q42-38.n: Consultation is a quality of the believing community, including consultation between spouses in household matters.

q18-23.n: Planning is required, with humility before a future that only Allah controls.

q17-36.n: Do not follow or build a judgement on what you do not know for certain; hearing, sight and the heart will all be questioned.

q39-36.n: A rhetorical question that cuts off the fear of people: Allah is sufficient for you.

q40-44.n: Said by the believer from Pharaoh's family after he had spoken the truth and feared the consequences: entrusting the matter to Allah after doing one's duty.

q6-17.n: Harm and benefit are in Allah's hand alone, so do not attach yourself to people in a way that enslaves the heart.

q35-2.n: What Allah has allotted you, no one can withhold, and what He withholds, no one can give — a cure for envy and anxiety about competitors.

q3-26.n: Positions and honour are in Allah's hand; He gives and takes them away. So let no one in a position be deluded, and let no one who lost it despair.

q11-88.n: Shu‘ayb said it: the reformer's aim is “as much as I am able”, and the result is by Allah's help.

q91-9.n: Success depends on purifying the soul, and failure lies in neglecting it and burying it in sins.

q79-40.n: Resisting one's desires is a sign of fearing Allah, and its reward is Paradise.

q12-53.n: Admitting the weakness of the self is not defeat but realism that protects from pride and pushes one to seek Allah's help.

q53-32.n: Do not praise yourself or declare yourself perfect; Allah knows best the reality of hearts.

q57-20.n: A precise description of the stages of attachment to this world, all of which end in debris — a cure for the race of comparison.

q3-185.n: Death is a shared reality, and true success is measured by the Hereafter, not by worldly standards.

q16-97.n: A good life is promised in this world before the next; the early scholars explained it as contentment, satisfaction and the sweetness of obedience.

q20-124.n: Inner tightness may be an effect of distance from Allah, even when material means are plentiful.

q2-152.n: The greatest companionship: that you remember Allah and He remembers you.

q4-28.n: Allah knows human weakness and wants to lighten things; the Shariah is mercy, not a burden.

q2-185.n: A universal principle: ease is an aim of the Shariah, and being harsh on oneself goes against what Allah wants.

q22-78.n: Removing hardship is a foundation of the Shariah — a cure for whisperings and excessive strictness.

q24-30.n: Lowering the gaze is the first step in guarding the heart and the body, and it is “purer” — cleaner and better for the soul.

q24-33.n: Keeping chaste through conscious effort while waiting for Allah's relief through marriage.

q17-32.n: The prohibition is of “approaching”, not only of the act: cutting off the paths that lead to it, such as seclusion, looking and private conversations.

q24-21.n: Going astray does not happen all at once but in steps; being aware of the first step is easier than resisting the last.

q29-45.n: Prayer with a present heart builds an inner barrier against indecency.

q5-90.n: The command to avoid is stronger than a bare prohibition: keep away from the whole environment.

q114-1.n: The whisperer “who withdraws” retreats when Allah is remembered; the cure is seeking refuge and turning away, not arguing with it.

q23-97.n: Seeking refuge from the promptings of Satan that stir up anger, desire and whisperings.

q59-18.n: Daily self-accounting: what have you put forward for tomorrow?

q103-1.n: Al-Shafi‘i said: Had Allah revealed no proof to His creation other than this surah, it would have sufficed them. Time is your capital, and salvation comes through four things.

q23-115.n: Your life has meaning and purpose; you were not created in vain, and everything you live through has weight.

q6-162.n: A single direction: when your whole life is for Allah, the weight of people's approval becomes lighter.

q4-29.n: Your soul is a trust, and Allah is merciful to you; ending the verse with mercy speaks to the one in pain before it speaks to the one at fault.

q2-195.n: Protecting oneself from destruction is obligatory, and this includes seeking treatment and rest.

q17-82.n: The Quran is a healing for hearts from doubts and worries, and this does not conflict with taking medical means.

q10-57.n: A healing for what is in the breasts: from worry, confusion and whisperings.

q26-80.n: Ibrahim's refinement: he attributed the illness to himself — “when I am ill” — and the healing to Allah.

q50-16.n: Allah is closer to you than anyone; there is no loneliness with this nearness.

q2-45.n: Prayer is heavy for the one without humility, but for the humble it is rest and refuge: “Give us rest through it, O Bilal.”

q7-56.n: Supplication is between fear and hope, and mercy is near to those who do good.

q33-21.n: The verse this app is built on: the Prophet ﷺ is a practical example in every human situation, for whoever hopes in Allah and remembers Him.

q68-4.n: ‘A'ishah was asked about his character and said: His character was the Quran (Muslim 746).

q9-128.n: The qualities of a merciful leader: it pains him when his followers suffer, and he is keen for their good.

q21-107.n: The mercy is for all the worlds: humans and animals, believers and others.

q18-28.n: Good company needs “patience” and a conscious choice, and it is one of the strongest causes of steadfastness.

q43-67.n: Every friendship not built on piety will turn into enmity on the Day of Resurrection.

q25-27.n: A warning against the companion who leads you away from Allah, even if he is dear to you.

q8-46.n: Internal dispute weakens any team, family or partnership and takes away its strength.

q3-103.n: Harmony after enmity is a blessing from Allah, to be asked of Him and preserved by holding fast together.

q3-8.n: A supplication for steadfastness: guidance is a blessing that needs constant protection.

q2-201.n: The supplication the Prophet ﷺ made most often, as Anas said (al-Bukhari 6389); it gathers the good of this world and the next.

q2-250.n: “Pour upon us” paints patience being poured out until it fills the heart.

q21-89.n: Zakariyya's supplication in his old age, asking for a child; while asking, he praised Allah as the best of inheritors, content with His decree.

q3-38.n: Zakariyya's supplication when he saw Allah's favour to Maryam: asking for “good” offspring, not just offspring.

q18-10.n: The supplication of the youths when they took refuge in the cave without a clear plan: they asked for mercy and right guidance.

q14-40.n: Ibrahim prays for himself and his offspring to establish prayer; upbringing is supplication before it is instructions.

q7-126.n: The supplication of the magicians who believed, when Pharaoh threatened them: they asked for patience and steadfastness until death.
